newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Annan says he believes U.S. will pay UN dues.
newsitem.headline: Annan says he believes U.S. will pay UN dues.

text.p: United Nations Secretary- General Kofi Annan said on Friday he believed the United States would pay its huge backlog of dues, partly because Americans did not like their country being seen as a "deadbeat."

Speaking at a news conference at the end of a three-day stay in Geneva, Annan indicated that talks he had with President Bill Clinton and members of Congress earlier this year had given him hope the at least $1 billion debt would be honoured.
"My own view is that we will get the money. How much and when, I cannot tell you, but the mood is changing. There is public debate on this issue," he said.
"Americans don't like to be in this situation. I don't think (they feel) it is dignified for the richest country in the world to be treated as the biggest deadbeat on these issues."

Annan, who was strongly supported for the top job by Washington when it vetoed his predecessor Boutros Boutros-Ghali for a second term last year, was using a phrase originally voiced by the former U.S. ambassador to the U.N. in Geneva.

The envoy, Daniel Spiegel, who returned to legal practice at the end of last year, was fiercely criticised in Congress after he suggested in a 1995 speech, standing alongside Boutros-Ghali, that his country was behaving like "a deadbeat dad".
In U.S. parlance, a "deadbeat" is someone who refuses to pay his debts, and a "deadbeat dad" is a father who avoids paying maintenance for his children.
Annan said Clinton and his administration were convinced that the U.N. was essential for the United States "and that if the U.S. expects to lead, it has to pay its dues."

Last month, new U.S. ambassador to the United Nations in New York Bill Richardson told Congress -- where scepticism about the value of the world body is strong -- that the dues had to be paid if the United States wanted to retain its influence there.
Paying up would also be vital if it were to finally win reforms, already launched by Annan, that would lead to a reduction in future U.S. dues, Richardson said.
The U.N. itself says the U.S. debt totals $1.6 billion, but Washington says it is just over $1 billion. The difference is due to a dispute over what should be included.
Annan, who in January had talks with Jesse Helms, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and a fierce critic of the U.N, said the world body had "good support" in the U.S. legislature.
"But there are important elements in Congress who do not seem to accept the relevance of the U.N.... And I think that some are running out of excuses not to pay," he added.

Ordinary U.S. citizens and "responsible Americans" were embarrassed by the situation, the U.N. chief said. "The debate is going on and I think we will put this behind us so that we can focus on the real issues."

Annan, a long-time U.N. official from Ghana, said he could not reform "and manage an efficient programme on a shoestring budget" -- although he was dedicated to reshaping the organisation as the U.S. has demanded.
But he said part of the reform "must be a commitment and rededication of member states to the ideals of the Organisation...."
But this should also include "a commitment from each and every one of them to meet their legal obligations and pay their contributions in full and on time," he added.
